BrixtonBuzz-2026-01-27#000.title: The Victoria tube line is officially the loudest in London (Brixton Buzz, 27 Jan 2026)
BrixtonBuzz-2026-01-27#000.text:
This won't come as much of a surprise to regular users of the Victoria line, but a new study has found that the stretch of line between Green Park and Victoria is positively deafening, registering a thundering 92.9 decibels – the loudest on the network.
Two other sections of the Victoria Line between Highbury & Islington and Finsbury Park, and Highbury & Islington to King's Cross St Pancras also made the top four biggest rackets, while Brixton to Stockwell was also a noisy offender.
The loudest sections of the London Underground
According to the TfL data, the highest recorded average noise levels in the dataset were found on the following station-to-station sections:
Green Park to Victoria (Victoria line) – 92.9 decibels
Liverpool Street to Bethnal Green (Central line) – 92.8 decibels
Highbury & Islington to Finsbury Park (Victoria line) – 92.1 decibels
Highbury & Islington to King's Cross St Pancras (Victoria line) – 91.5 decibels
Gants Hill to Newbury Park (Central line) – 91.1 decibels
For context, normal conversation typically occurs at around 60 decibels, meaning passengers travelling through these sections may find it difficult to speak without raising their voices.
Sound levels above 90 decibels are commonly compared to everyday noises such as a motorcycle engine, a lawnmower, heavy traffic, or a loud live music venue.
Public health guidance commonly notes that prolonged or repeated exposure to sounds above 85 decibels can increase the risk of hearing damage over time.
While individual Tube journeys are typically short, commuters who regularly travel on the loudest sections of the Underground may experience repeated exposure to higher noise levels, particularly during peak travel hours.
Deep-level lines dominate the loudest rankings
The data shows that the Victoria and Central lines appear most frequently among the loudest sections recorded. These are both deep-level lines, which operate through narrower tunnels and often feature tighter curves.
Other high-noise sections in the data also include:
Wanstead to Redbridge (Central line) – 90.7 decibels
Brixton to Stockwell (Victoria line) – 90.1 decibels
Camden Town to Euston (Northern line) – 89.8 decibels
Pimlico to Victoria (Victoria line) – 89.6 decibels
Why noise varies so much on the Tube
Noise levels on the Underground vary by section rather than by line alone. The TfL recordings show that even short journeys between stations can produce significantly different results, influenced by factors such as tunnel depth, curvature, speed, and track condition.
As a result, two journeys on the same line can feel very different in terms of how easy it is to hold a conversation.
Daniel de Nieuwe, Head of Product from JRPass said:
"The London Underground is one of the world's oldest metro systems, and this data shows just how much noise levels can vary depending on where you're travelling.
People aren't imagining it – some Tube stretches are averaging above 90 decibels. On those sections, even a quick conversation can turn into shouting.

Tube noise
• Tube noise is a longstanding issue for TfL, and we have well established
processes in place to mitigate it as far as possible
• We invest significant time and resources into our Tube noise-focused track
works. In the last 5 years, we have spent approximately £7-10m a year on rail
grinding (for both critical maintenance needs and noise reduction), and over the
last year have carried out over 30,000m of rail grinding specifically for noise
reduction
• We review and respond to every complaint we receive
• We have to balance our interventions to manage both residential and in-tunnel
noise, which affects train operators and customers
• There are a number of known hotspots across London that we manage primarily
through the use of regular rail grinding

services in 2016
[p.4]
Two main types of noise issue: residential and
in-tunnel
• In-tunnel noise: impacts both train
operators and our customers
• Residential noise: impacts our
neighbours living and working close to
the railway
• Balancing the two: we have to balance
mitigations for in-tunnel and
residential noise, as these can
sometimes conflict. Mitigations for
one may make the other worse. We
are working on solutions now which
manage both effectively
[p.5]
Causes
Longwave corrugation (rail roughness) is
caused by repeated acceleration and braking,
and is more prevalent on the lines using
automatic train operation. There is less
corrugation on the manually driven lines
which have more speed variation (Bakerloo
and Piccadilly lines). Longwave corrugation
tends to translate into residential noise.
Longwave Corrugation
Shortwave corrugation is caused in the same
way as longwave corrugation, but tends to
result in in-tunnel noise for train operators and
customers.
Shortwave Corrugation

Causes
Curves and the manner in which the
trains operate around these also play a
role in the type of corrugation created,
and could result in a screeching sound
in-tunnel and/or for residents.
Insulated Rail Joints
In some cases, residential noise complaints are
also related to impulsive noise caused by trains
passing over track infrastructure, including:
• Insulated rail joints - part of older signalling
systems to enable signalling sections
• Points and crossings - enables trains to traverse
from one set of tracks to another
• Voiding sleepers
• Rail defects
Points and Crossings

FOI-1730-1819#000.title: Cleaning of Central line to stop vibration noise; Rail Roughness Plots BEG-MIE January 2018
FOI-1730-1819#000.text:
FOI request detail
cleaning of central line to stop vibration noise
Request ID: FOI-1730-1819
Date published: 22 October 2018
You asked
Please provide information regarding the work done on the Central Line between Bethnal Green and Mile End in the past year to prevent noise and vibration.
If no work has been done to reduce vibration and noise in the past year please provide information as to when this will be done.
Please provide information regarding monitoring of noise and vibration on the Central Line between Bethnal Green and Mile End.
We answered
Dear
TfL Ref: FOI-1730-1819
Thank you for your email received by Transport for London (TfL) on 30 September 2018.
Your request has been considered in accordance with the requirements of the Freedom of Information Act and our information access policy. I can confirm we hold some of the information you require. You asked:
Please provide information regarding the work done on the Central Line between Bethnal Green and Mile End in the past year to prevent noise and vibration.
This is one of the locations
where current technology and the age of the track mean that
it is not technically practicable to reduce the noise and vibration any further. However we
are continuing to investigate and monitor the noise on this stretch of the line, but the unique and historic infrastructure of the London Underground makes noise reduction very challenging.
Where it is practicable to reduce noise, we do – and we have reduced the noise for hundreds of properties affected by rail noise.
If no work has been done to reduce vibration and noise in the past year please provide information as to when this will be done.
Whilst rail grinding is not deemed as an engineering method to reduce noise, some residents have experienced a reduction in noise levels following grinding. Rail grinding is primarily undertaken to reduce the growth rate of cracks and to improve the wheel-rail interface which can cause noise.
We will undertake rail grinding at this location in February 2019, with the intention to improve the wheel-rail interface. There may be a reduction in noise level however this is not guaranteed.
Please provide information regarding monitoring of noise and vibration on the Central Line between Bethnal Green and Mile End.
Please find the attached rail roughness of the area for your information. The rail roughness measurements confirm an elevated rail roughness levels between 720 and 880m which are the likely cause of the noise at this site. Rail roughness is caused by general wear and tear.
Furthermore, the noise
measurements in the below tables are from residential properties in the vicinity of the location in question.
If this is not the information you are looking for, or if you are unable to access it for some reason, please do not hesitate to contact me.
Please see the attached information sheet for details of your right to appeal as well as information on copyright and what to do if you would like to re-use any of the information we have disclosed.
Yours sincerely
Eva Hextall
FOI Case Officer
FOI Case Management Team
General Counsel
Transport for London

FOI-2986-2324#000.title: Central line noise: Central line cab recordings (September 2023)
FOI-2986-2324#000.text:
FOI request detail
Central line noise
Request ID: FOI-2986-2324
Date published: 12 December 2023
You asked
I'm working on an acoustic panel attempting to target and reduce the noise level inside the central tube underground. However, I need some critical information from TFL to understand better and design acoustic solutions.
Here are some of my questions:
1. Is the noise produced inside the central line tube mainly high frequency or low frequency? Or is it a mix of them? What is the ratio of the two kinds of noise produced inside the tube?
2. What's the noise frequency range?
3. What is the inside wall of the central line tube made of?
4. What is the current highest noise level inside the train?
5. What are some inside-tube noise reduction TFL has planned to do?
6. Are there any research opportunities for me to join or further investigate?
We answered
TfL Ref: FOI-2986-2324
Thank you for your request which we received on 4 November 2023, asking about noise levels on the Central line.
Your request has been considered in accordance with the requirements of the Environmental Information Regulations (EIRs) and our information access policy. I can confirm that we hold the information you require.
You specifically asked:
Is the noise produced inside the central line tube mainly high frequency or low frequency? Or is it a mix of them? What is the ratio of the two kinds of noise produced inside the tube?
What's the noise frequency range?
The attached table, which contains data taken on 4 September 2023, provides the levels and 1/3rd octaves in a Central line train cab recorded for the entire tunnel sections between White City and Newbury Park.
What is the inside wall of the central line tube made of?
It's steel rings and concrete.
What is the current highest noise level inside the train?
See the attached table.
What are some inside-tube noise reduction TFL has planned to do?
We want to tackle in-carriage Tube noise by removing certain track fastenings linked to increased noise levels, and either replacing with alternative track fastenings, or installing new rail. We are exploring the use of variable speeds to understand the impact on the growth of corrugation. However, rail grinding is our primary method of addressing in-carriage levels.
Are there any research opportunities for me to join or further investigate? We don't have anyone trying to research this topic, so I am not sure, but I wonder if Anthony and Chris feel this is something they could support from an engineering perspective?
We don't have a study on in-carriage Tube noise on the London Underground at the moment. I have passed your email onto my colleagues who deal with this issue for their attention.
If this is not the information you are looking for, or if you are unable to access it for any reason, please do not hesitate to contact me.
Please see the attached information sheet for details of your right to appeal as well as information on copyright and what to do if you would like to re-use any of the information we have disclosed.
Yours sincerely
Eva Hextall
FOI Case Management Team
General Counsel
Transport for London

MQ-2022-1791#000.title: Mayor's Question 2022/1791 Tube Noise (2): sections ground for noise Dec 2021-May 2022 and planned grinding
MQ-2022-1791#000.text:
London Assembly
Tube Noise (2)
Meeting: | MQT on 23 June 2022
Session name: | MQT on 23/06/2022 between 10:00 and 13:00
Reference: | 2022/1791
Question by: | Caroline Pidgeon
Organisation: | Liberal Democrats
Asked of: | The Mayor
Category: | Transport
Question
Tube Noise (2)
Please set out which sections of the London Underground have benefited from grinding of the railway lines to help reduce noise levels in the last six months. Please also set out the specific geographical locations that will benefit from grinding over the next six months.
Answer
Date:
Tuesday 28 June 2022
While the primary purpose of rail grinding on the Tube network is safety and operational reliability by managing rail defects, and maximising asset life, it is also used for the purpose of noise reduction.
The requested information is in the attached spreadsheet. Please note that the rail grinding programme for the next six months is still provisional (and TfL also expects additional sites to be added) and remains subject to change dependent on operational requirements.
Rail grinding for the purpose of noise reduction is reviewed in order to ensure benefits are maximised. Where rail roughness levels are higher, the benefits of rail grinding are likely to be greater in terms of noise reduction.

MQ-2022-2799#000.title: Mayor's Question 2022/2799 Outstanding Rail Grinding Works - Tube Noise
MQ-2022-2799#000.text:
London Assembly
Outstanding Rail Grinding Works – Tube Noise
Meeting: | MQT on 15 September 2022
Session name: | MQT on 15/09/2022 between 10:00 and 13:00
Reference: | 2022/2799
Question by: | Caroline Pidgeon
Organisation: | Liberal Democrats
Asked of: | The Mayor
Category: | Transport
Question
Outstanding Rail Grinding Works – Tube Noise
With reference to your answer to question 2022/1791, please provide dates for completion for each of the outstanding railway grinding works.
Answer
Date:
Wednesday 21 September 2022
Officers are preparing an answer.
Date:
Tuesday 20 December 2022
I can confirm that all Central, Northern and Jubilee line sections included in the planned grinding list in
Mayor's Question 2022/1791
have now been completed, with the exception of Balham to Clapham South, which Transport for London (TfL) was unable to carry out before the rail grinding machine was required on a different Tube line, due to traction current issues. TfL will look to carry out rail grinding on this section of track when further grinding is carried out on the Northern line next year. TfL carried out grinding on the Victoria line in October and November 2022, including between Highbury & Islington and King's Cross St. Pancras, as set out in
Mayor's Question 2022/1791
.
TfL's continuous rail grinding programme is confirmed around eight weeks in advance of works, with safety and operationally critical work prioritised. Once grinding to address defects has been scheduled and spare capacity identified, grinding to address noise and vibration can be planned.

Elly Baker AM
What action is TfL taking to reduce harmful noise levels on the London Underground?
Sir Sadiq Khan (Mayor of London): Good morning, thanks for your question. I recognise the impact that
noise can have on people travelling on the London Underground and those residents who live in close
proximity to it. That is one of the reasons I am grateful for the Member being assiduous in following up on this
matter on a regular basis.
The principal cause of track noise is rail corrugation and Transport for London (TfL) carries out regular grinding
of the track to manage this. Given the negative impact this can have on users and residents, I have introduced
a dedicated rail grinding budget giving TfL access to £9 million in 2025/26, up from £8.1 million in 2024/25.
This, alongside improved grinding efficiency, is allowing TfL to be more productive in tackling rail corrugation.
There is, I should add, a significant backlog of works caused by the lack of funding from the previous
Government and the legacy of the pandemic. Nevertheless, and despite the uplift in TfL funding from this
Government, it remains the case that TfL resources are constrained. That is why TfL uses a data-led approach
to target its grinding efforts where they are most needed.
In addition to grinding, TfL is continuing to investigate alternative solutions to manage Tube noise. TfL is
installing resilient base plates as part of their track renewal programme which can help reduce vibration. TfL
has also been trialling speed variation whereby trains vary their speed on curves prone to specific types of
corrugation. This has had some success on the Victoria line and TfL is investigating the possibility of expanding
this practice to other lines.
TfL also looks to learn extensively from the practices of other metro network operators around the world.
However, the London Underground is not only large, it is also far older than any other metro system in the
world and has unique infrastructure challenges. That is why TfL has my full support in its efforts to explore
innovative tech solutions to solve this issue. One new piece of technology is an acoustic focused rail grinding
machine which is due to be trialled in tunnels later this year. If successful, this could be included in TfL's
grinding contract from late 2027 and may assist track grinding in areas with more limited ventilation.

MQT-2026-2156#001.title: Mayor's Question Time 16 July 2026, Question 2026/2156 Tube Noise (Elly Baker AM), transcript
MQT-2026-2156#001.text:
[p.1]
I want to assure Londoners that I understand the significant impact that high levels of Tube noise can have and
that is why I expect TfL to continue to address all noise complaints with the seriousness they deserve.
Elly Baker AM: Thanks very much, Mr Mayor. I appreciate the genuine acknowledgement and concern you
have shown to those affected by noise and vibration in their homes. It is the residential noise and vibration
that I want to focus on and I would really like to emphasise also the impact living with noise and vibration of
[p.2]
trains going under your house every few minutes in their homes, coming through walls, beds, floors, in some
cases all night, can have a huge impact on sleep and obviously that has a resulting impact for many on their
mental health. Londoners in general will be quite shocked if they knew in those homes where they are affected
how bad it can be.
I would also like to acknowledge, and I am sure all residents affected would as well, this is obviously a genuine
and complex problem. No one expects this to be solved overnight. The solutions in each case are also very
complex. The feedback we get, and for those Assembly Members who are dealing with this on a regular basis,
is that TfL's approach is not getting better, it is worsening. I would like to specifically say, last month I wrote to
Andy Lord [Commissioner of TfL] direct. In that letter I asked for a significant improvement in the quality and
quantity of data. I asked for specific data based on the residents' casework that we dealt with. An improvement
in the quality and quantity of data shared with Assembly Members and therefore that could be shared with the
residents to monitor the issue, look at the measures being taken and specifics on complaints.
Last week, I received an email, not from Andy Lord - I did not get a letter back from Andy Lord, despite the
fact we put a lot of effort into that letter, making sure it was really comprehensive - just an email from TfL's
Government Relations turning down the majority of the requests for data. It contained the reassuring phrase,
"We are fully committed to tackling Tube noise, but – as you have said – resources remain constrained". I have
to say that catch-all phrase that anyone dealing with Tube noise, it strikes horror into your heart, the data-led
approach. If there is all this data, I do not quite know why they cannot just share it with us.
But there is the contradiction, they say they are fully committed but that resources are constrained. From
where I am sitting over the last five years that I have been an Assembly Member; I do not feel that TfL is
adequately allocating resources to this issue that genuinely is causing misery for a group of Londoners. You
have said about the rail grinding budget and that is good. I will talk more about the data as well so that we can
see the impact of that. Can you commit again to looking at the overall allocation of resources it uses to
manage the issue of Tube noise?

MQT-2026-2156#002.title: Mayor's Question Time 16 July 2026, Question 2026/2156 Tube Noise (Elly Baker AM), transcript
MQT-2026-2156#002.text:
[p.2]
Sir Sadiq Khan (Mayor of London): Chair, can I say there is not a lot the Member has said that I would
disagree with in terms of how unacceptable it is. I am particularly sensitive to the misery this causes those
residents affected by this. Just so that she is aware, we have also been contacted in my office by
Assembly Member Hirani, Assembly Member Ahmad, Assembly Member Moema, and
Assembly Member Cooper, frustrated like you at the lack of proactiveness on the part of TfL.
A couple of things just to say by way of background, not as a rebuttal. There was progress being made in terms
of dealing with this issue in the years leading up to the pandemic. I have figures for the amount of money
invested. That in itself is not a good criteria because you can become more efficient and spend less money.
Then there was a massive plummeting of maintenance work in terms of pounds and pence spent, which is one
of the reasons why things are and appear to be worse subsequently because you have had the years of inaction
and so forth, and we hope to improve that.
The substantive point she makes is in relation to the lack of transparency. That is an easier problem to solve, I
would say, than the issue of the technology to solve the problem. I know as a consequence of my suggestion,
TfL meets every few months with Members of the Assembly. What I will do is ensure that the information it
provides is far, far, far more detailed than is currently received. In prepping for this over the weekend, I looked
at what information it provides. I will make sure it provides, in addition, information on what in real-time rail
grinding activity is taking place over the next six months, the track renewal programmes, alternative noise
reduction measures that are being considered or in delivery. As she said, a constituency-level breakdown,
[p.3]
which is really important, of the noise level complaints and what action is being taken. I am more than happy
to get that in train – forgive the pun – as soon as possible, because, as I said, the substance is one issue, but
the lack of transparency is a very easily solvable issue. My promise to her is I will make sure today I speak to
the Commissioner's team to try to get some movement there.
Elly Baker AM: Thanks. I do really appreciate that. I would like to just emphasise why it is important, though,
because it just feels like TfL does not recognise the value clear data on the issue has for residents. They are
living with it every day. They understand it, to be honest, probably better than TfL in some cases, and they
want a dialogue that says, "This is working, this is not", not in real time, but as it is happening, rather than
waiting, frankly, months for responses and then, when the responses come back, they do not answer the
questions the residents have asked. They will give a general picture of what is going on.

MQT-2026-2156#003.title: Mayor's Question Time 16 July 2026, Question 2026/2156 Tube Noise (Elly Baker AM), transcript
MQT-2026-2156#003.text:
[p.3]
Those experiences, that genuine engagement makes such a difference. I was elected 2021 in the pandemic
already; we were already seeing those restrictions on funding. Something has happened in terms of the way it
deals with these complaints and its openness, and it is not just about funding, although I do think we need to
look at the resources. It is that approach, for instance, you have mentioned a forward plan of rail grinding for
six months that I asked, the response I have says, "We cannot do that because it is only planned eight weeks in
advance". Fine. Did it offer to tell us eight weeks in advance? No, it just did not answer that at all. It is that
approach that makes residents – and frankly us – think that TfL is trying to hide what it is doing.
Tell us what it is doing. Let us see. No one thinks this is easy. We just want to work together. If you can really
emphasise to TfL that transparency, but also in terms of its response to residents, be specific, be open, and
honestly, if it does not have enough people to respond in decent time, then it needs to put more people on it
because this is not going away.
Sir Sadiq Khan (Mayor of London): Yes, Chair, I also take away from this – by the way, again, there is
nothing she said that I disagree with – this is a canary in the mine. If TfL is not responding to Members of the
Assembly with information and transparency in a manner that is befitting, it begs the question, is it responding
to residents in terms of this? It is really important for us to proceed.
I will write to the Assembly, if that is OK, because I suspect it is an issue for all Members of the Assembly in
relation to a forward programme of meetings with the Assembly, what additional information will be provided,
and I cannot see a reason why the eight weeks programme cannot be provided. I take the point about when
you get the tracks and stuff, but, Chair, let me take this away with your permission and come back to all the
Assembly. Can I end how I began by thanking the Member for the assiduous way she has dealt with this, but
also the collegiate way she wants to move forward. As I said, we all want TfL to succeed. We cannot afford
residents having this misery when it can be ameliorated.
Elly Baker AM: Much appreciated. Thanks. We may talk about this again, I am sure. Maybe even to just say
that it has improved, that would be positive, would it not? Back to you, Chair.
Andrew Boff AM (Chair): I am pretty certain we will be talking about this again, not just maybe. The next
question is entitled Changing your Mind from Assembly Member Wilson.

TfL-noise-update-2024-08#000.title: TfL Tube Noise: January to June 2024 update to London Assembly Members (Claire Mann, 9 Aug 2024)
TfL-noise-update-2024-08#000.text:
[p.1]
Appendix 7a
Claire Mann
9 August 2024 Chief Operating Officer
Transport for London
Palestra
London Assembly Members
197 Blackfriars Road
London
SE1 8NJ
Sent via email only
Dear Members of the London Assembly,
Tube Noise: January to June 2024 update
I am writing to provide the latest update on our work to address noise and vibration
across the Tube network. I am pleased to follow the work of my predecessor Glynn
Barton, who I know worked closely with you on this issue during his time as Chief
Operating Officer. I look forward to continuing this, collaborating with you closely to
deliver improvements for residents and passengers on noise and vibration from the
London Underground.
I understand that some members of the Assembly are interested in a verbal briefing
on the issue of Tube noise as a whole, and that some new members will not have
yet been briefed on it by TfL. If this is something you would like arranged, please get
in touch with the Government Relations team via
memberscorrespondence@tfl.gov.uk and we would be happy to set up a session.
This update covers the months of January-June 2024. As referenced in my previous
letter in February, updates cover spans of six calendar months, from January to
June, and from July to December, so as to be easily comparable. We will aim to
deliver these to you within six weeks of the period concluding.
We continue to prioritise tackling corrugated rails, which are the principal contributor
to Tube noise. We address this primarily through rail grinding, which works to
smooth the tracks. We have continued to carry out a comprehensive programme of
rail grinding to tackle noise and vibration in locations across the network. This has
covered different lines and locations on the network where we know grinding plays a
role in reducing corrugation and Tube noise.
We have also continued our work to mitigate in-carriage noise issues regarding the
installation of Pandrol Vanguard (PV).
• We have completed PV conversion to Delkor as part of Deep Tube
Reconditioning at seven locations
[p.2]
• Nine sites are in the process of Deep Tube Reconditioning, with a further
three planned to begin this financial year
• We have removed PV and replaced rails at two sites
• At the remaining sites, we continue to plan works to address PV-related
issues, dependent on operational capacity and impact on tunnel noise
We continue to work with our Open Innovation team to explore how we might deliver
innovative solutions in the realm of Tube noise. We hope to be able to share an
update with Members in due course.
Furthermore, we have removed redundant and noise-creating joints at sites on
multiple lines, which helps to reduce impulsive noise. As part of this work, we repack
and consolidate ballast to ensure stable trackbeds and mitigate noise levels.

TfL-noise-update-2024-08#001.title: TfL Tube Noise: January to June 2024 update to London Assembly Members (Claire Mann, 9 Aug 2024)
TfL-noise-update-2024-08#001.text:
[p.2]
We continue with our plans for a trial involving absorbent material installation
between North Greenwich and Canning Town. We have appointed a contractor and
will meet with them in the coming months to plan timescales for this trial.
We continue to work to understand how the speed of our trains impacts rail
degradation and hence Tube noise.
The variable speed trial which we began in 2023 on the Northern line between
Tufnell Park and Kentish Town has seen some success. In this trial, at a location
where there is currently PV still in place, trains run at slower speeds between Friday
and Sunday, and at normal speed for the rest of the week. This is to reduce the
repetitive movements on the rail and hence corrugation, which should in turn reduce
the noise experienced by passengers in the train, and residents who live nearby.
Following initial success, the trial has been extended to between Camden Town and
Kentish Town, enabling us to capture more data of differing track types and layouts
where corrugation is an issue. We are happy to keep you updated as the trial
progresses.
Work is ongoing with Schweerbau, the manufacturer of our grinding trains. We are
looking into how we might trial their new acoustic grinding train which is claimed to
better manage noise-related corrugation and grind greater distances. We hope,
constraints permitting, to trial this in the current financial year.
We are also looking to trial Tuned Mass Dampers in the 2024/25 financial year.
These are technologies which aim to lower in-tunnel noise and slow corrugation
growth. We are seeking quotes from the two main global suppliers, and further
information on timescales for this trial will be available later this year.
Please find below further updates on known noise hotspot locations which you may
find useful:
[p.3]
Jubilee line
Kingsbury Curve
Grinding continues to prove an effective strategy in reducing noise at this
location. Measurements carried out in early 2024 indicated noise reductions
and we continue to grind as appropriate. The next grinding will take place over
the summer of 2024, and we expect this to reduce noise levels significantly.
St Johns Wood – Baker Street
We continue to undertake grinding in this area. We previously replaced PV
with Delkor on the northbound track in 2021. We began the same process on
the southbound track in spring 2024, to reduce in-carriage noise, and expect
this to be completed in 2025. We made residents aware that during works
noise and vibration might be more noticeable as the track fastenings were
removed and then reinstalled.
Separately, we became aware of a localised issue regarding a failing track
baseplate, requiring a bespoke design. Additional track renewal and repair
works to optimise the functioning of the new baseplate took place in late 2024,
and this proved successful. As a result of this work, noise levels have
improved at this location.

TfL-noise-update-2024-08#002.title: TfL Tube Noise: January to June 2024 update to London Assembly Members (Claire Mann, 9 Aug 2024)
TfL-noise-update-2024-08#002.text:
[p.3]
Northern line
Archway – Highgate
We have identified higher levels of corrugation in this area, and are looking to
add this location to our grinding programme to help improve the track
condition.
Kennington loop
The new rail installed late in 2023 is keeping this section at a low level of
corrugation. We updated residents on these works as we were carrying them
out. We undertook a track walk in early 2024 which did not identify any
additional likely causes of noise beyond corrugation, which we are addressing
as part of our grinding programme.
Kennington to Waterloo
Having received resident feedback of rumbling, we are arranging for rail
grinding to take place. We have previously resolved a rail defect and replaced
sleepers this year.
South Wimbledon
Our previous COO Glynn Barton wrote to former AM Pidgeon earlier this year.
In our efforts to investigate the causes of noise at this location we have
carried out visits to the location this year. We carried out trackside monitoring
[p.4]
in June, which identified corrugation which has been subsequently ground.
Further grinding will take place in the autumn using the grinding train. We are
also expecting to meet AM Cooper at this site later this year.
Victoria line
Finsbury Park – Seven Sisters
We have continued to use grinding to manage corrugation and noise in this
area. Grinding took place in July 2024 on the southbound track.
Kings Cross St Pancras – Highbury & Islington
Our data-led approach in this area continues, enabling us to best focus our
resources on specific parts of this section of track where higher levels of
corrugation are present. We continue to communicate with residents and
other stakeholders, and have met with them alongside the Deputy Mayor for
Transport to discuss our strategy. Unfortunately, we were unable to deliver
some planned grinding in March, which has contributed to higher noise levels.
We have apologised to residents for this, and in addition to grinding of part of
this section in May, are working to add the sections missed to our forthcoming
grinding programme as soon as possible.
Pimlico
Delkor installation continues and is expected to be completed this year, as
part of ongoing Deep Tube Reconditioning.
Stockwell – Vauxhall
We have trialled different approaches following the removal of PV in this
location. We are assessing whether removing it and not replacing it improves
track condition. Initial assessments are that it has reduced the need for
grinding, which will be carried out when it is required to reduce rail roughness
levels.
Walthamstow Central – Blackhorse Road
We expect to complete the flat-bottom conversion of the rail at this location
later this year. We are taking measurements at properties in the area to allow
us to assess the impact this conversion is having on noise levels.

TfL-noise-update-2025-08#000.title: TfL Tube Noise Update: January to July 2025 to London Assembly Members (Claire Mann, 20 Aug 2025)
TfL-noise-update-2025-08#000.text:
[p.1]
Appendix 12
Claire Mann
Chief Operating Officer
20 August 2025
Transport for London
London Assembly Members
Palestra
197 Blackfriars Road
Sent via email only London
SE1 8NJ
Dear Members of the London Assembly,
Tube Noise Update: January to July 2025
I write to update you on our ongoing work to address noise and vibration levels
across the London Underground network.
I know that noise and vibration levels remain an important issue for the
Assembly, and I would like to thank Members for their continued engagement
with us while we work hard to mitigate the effects on the Londoners we all serve.
Since my last update, our dedicated noise and vibration team here at Transport
for London (TfL) has continued to encourage innovation in this space – exploring
long term solutions while minimising noise and vibration levels through a tailored
programme of engineering solutions, including rail grinding. As previously
outlined, rail corrugation has been identified as the main cause of noise and
vibration across the London Underground network, and we employ a data-led
approach to tackle its growth. This approach analyses data from the entire
network to determine where rail defects occur and establish where corrugation
has worsened, allowing us to tailor and prioritise rail grinding schedules and other
engineering interventions accordingly.
At present, our work is centred around how we overcome a range of challenges
to ensure targeted and meaningful interventions can be made quickly and
effectively. These include changes in how services are operated to accommodate
line upgrades (like new trains and signalling equipment), and issues associated
with aging track infrastructure. As our fleet and infrastructure grow older, we have
seen an increase in rail defects, and more frequent recurrences of rail roughness
across the network. Consequently, demand for rail grinding to take place has
grown significantly, while budget allocations, resource and access constraints still
present barriers my team are working hard to manage.
While we continue to tackle the above, we are also committed to finding long-term solutions applicable across the London Underground network. By engaging
the market and drawing upon knowledge shared within the Community of Metros
(COMET), we have kept abreast of best practice measures employed by other
[p.2]
metro systems and positioned ourselves to work collaboratively with academia
where any advances are to be made.
In my last update, I outlined our ongoing work to seek effective technological
solutions and improve our response to the growing demand for rail grinding. I am
pleased to share that, through market engagement, an acoustic grinding train is
now in the final stages of approval. The train – which is said to increase grinding
output and reduce the need for ventilation with its hybrid-powered function – is on
track to undergo trialling across the Victoria and Northern lines this autumn. If the
train is successful, we will work collaboratively with suppliers to enter a contract
allowing us to employ this method on a regular basis.

TfL-noise-update-2025-08#001.title: TfL Tube Noise Update: January to July 2025 to London Assembly Members (Claire Mann, 20 Aug 2025)
TfL-noise-update-2025-08#001.text:
[p.2]
I also touched upon the progress of a Tuned Mass Damper product trial. Over the
last six months, operational colleagues identified issues affecting the functioning
of the product. Safety is our number one priority, and we have raised this issue
with the relevant supplier to ensure anything we trial on the network meets our
established safety standards. The supplier has since made amendments to the
product's design, so we can move forward with fitting the damper at Bank station
as part of the initial phase of the product trial.
I mentioned in February that we were exploring the use of variable speeds as a
noise mitigation measure. Signalling methods vary by line, and we are exploring
how we can best incorporate variable speeds into distinct signalling procedures
and requirements to suit different infrastructure. Similarly, we have been
exploring the effectiveness of 'coasting' as a measure to reduce noise and
vibration levels in some locations, and while we are still evaluating this method,
we have seen some positive results so far.
I recognise that the issue of noise and vibration is important to you and your
constituents, and we are committed to minimising any adverse effects on our
customers. Should any Member of the Assembly like a bespoke briefing on
issues within their constituency, please contact our Government Relations team
via memberscorrespondence@tfl.gov.uk and we would be happy to arrange this.
To aid us in reducing noise and vibration levels through our rail grinding
programme, I kindly ask Assembly Members to direct any noise complaints made
by constituents to our dedicated customer services team. Complaints made to
the TfL Contact Centre are carefully logged and tracked, and are used to help us
paint an accurate picture of noise and vibration levels across the network. If we
receive this information through various mediums, it becomes difficult to target
problem areas or 'hotspots' accordingly. The TfL Contact Centre can be
contacted by calling 0343 222 1234, or by visiting https://tfl.gov.uk/help-and-contact/contact-us-about-tube-and-rail. You may wish to flag that these
complaints have been made with our Government Relations team by contacting
the email address above.
Please find updates on known noise 'hotspot' locations which you may find useful
below.
[p.3]
Victoria line
Highbury & Islington to King's Cross St. Pancras
The Deputy Mayor, Seb Dance, Assembly Members Moema and Russell,
local residents and our noise and vibration specialists have engaged
continuously to address the root cause of recurring noise and vibration
issues in the area and drive forward mitigation measures. As part of this
work, planned rail grinding took place between 24-29 June and on 15 July
in the southbound direction, and 1010m-2260m of track was ground. Our
principal track engineer then carried out a detailed track inspection in both
the Northbound and southbound directions and found that some of the
timber sleepers have shrunk over time. A small gap between the concrete
and sleepers has thus emerged, and resulting micromovements have
exacerbated existing corrugation on the rail surface. Once available, the
findings from the report will be shared with Assembly Members and
residents. The Deputy Mayor is set to visit a local resident's home on 3
September – after this report has been shared – to listen to the questions
and concerns of those affected.

6. Raise suggestions to improve the web form for submitting noise complaints to TfL at the
next monthly steering group
This year, we have added a section to our main Help & Contacts page on our website titled 'Tube,
Rail, Overground, DLR, Trams, stations – Noise and vibration', which makes it easier for both
customers and residents to report noise and vibration concerns.
We have also edited the reporting page to prompt website users to report the date and time of not
only travel but Tube noise occurrences, making it clearer that Tube noise issues affecting residents
as well as passengers can be reported.

The work at Cockfosters is being carried out in preparation for the arrival of the new Piccadilly line

9. Share the current acoustic report on noise experienced on the Jubilee and Victoria lines
Acronyms:
• LEP,d- Daily Personal Exposure Level
• LAeq- Equivalent Continuous Sound Pressure Level
• LEAV- Lower Exposure Action Value
• UEAV- Upper Exposure Action Value
• ELV- Exposure Limit Value
[p.8]
We are committed to reducing in-carriage noise levels, which are managed primarily through rail
grinding and, where possible, by our deep Tube reconditioning programme, which is set out in
greater detail in answer 5.
The noise data was analysed with respect to The Control of Noise at Work Regulations 2005
(CNAWR), specifically:
• the 'lower exposure action value', corresponding to a daily personal noise exposure level of
80 dB(A);
• the 'upper exposure action value', corresponding to a daily personal noise exposure level of
85 dB(A);
• and the 'exposure limit value', corresponding to a daily personal noise exposure level of 87
dB(A).
Acoustic report for Victoria and Jubilee lines
Victoria line
In March 2021, Occupational Health noise exposure measurements were taken on the Victoria line.
11 end to end journeys were surveyed, with the average levels ranging between 81dB and 85dB,
and the highest peak level of 119dB. It is concluded that:
• Noise levels equal to or greater than 85 dB(A) (Median LAeq) were measured at ten
interstation sections
• The lower exposure action values (LEPd 80 dB(A)) could be reached or exceeded
• Noise exposure for all Train Operator duties are unlikely to reach the upper exposure action
values (LEPd 85 dB(A)) or the exposure limit values (LEPd 87 dB(A))
• No peak action or limit would be reached or exceeded during normal operations
Jubilee line
In February 2021, Occupational Health noise exposure measurements were taken on the Jubilee
line. Seven end-to-end journeys were surveyed, with the average levels ranging between 81 dB to
83 dB; the highest peak level was 119dB. It is concluded that:
• Higher noise levels were measured during travel through tunnel sections compared to
surface sections
• Noise levels greater than 85 dB(A) (Median LAeq) were measured at 11 interstation sections
• The lower exposure action values (LEPd 80 dB(A)) could be reached or marginally exceeded
for some duties
• Noise exposure for all Train Operator duties are unlikely to reach the UEAV (LEP,d 85 dB(A))
or the ELV (LEP,d 87 dB(A))
• No peak action or limit would be reached or exceeded during normal operations
